thread.title: Why Mean Can Be Nice In The Stock Market | Investor's Business Daily

author: PAUL WHITFIELD
title: Why Mean Can Be Nice In The Stock Market | Investor's Business Daily
text:
When the stock market reaches a certain level of meanness, IBD-style investors cheer additional losses for a technical reason. A major index signals a bear market when it drops 20% or more off its high.
X And a bear market resets the base count for all stocks. Why is this a big deal? Consider the stock market of 2011.
In August 2011, Apple ( AAPL ) was working on a risky fourth-stage base. IBD-style investors generally restrict buys to first- and second-stage stories. But Apple was about to get a gift.
How Apple Got A Break Before The Breakout The NYSE composite dropped 20% off its high in August 2011, eventually falling 26% by September 2011. The Nasdaq fell slightly more than 20% around that time, too. Apple, along with the rest of the stock market, was back to first-stage status. (Apple broke out several months later as a first-stage breakout. The stock gained 44% in less than four months.)
In the current stock market, the Nasdaq has come closest to the 20% loss level. The index has fallen as much as 18.3% off its high and is now about that much off the high, as of Tuesday's close. A couple of more bumps could leave the Nasdaq in bear market country.
Government Sales Crucial To Kratos Stocks such as Kratos Defense & Security Solutions ( KTOS ) could benefit. Kratos formed a third-stage base from September 2017 to September 2018. Although no one expects Kratos to be another Apple, it is a stock that could have more left to it. In another twist, the yearlong base is long enough that it can be considered to have reset Kratos' base count.
The company, known until 2007 as Wireless Facilities, is based in San Diego. At the time of the change, the company said "the name change reflects its revised focus as a leading defense contractor and security systems integrator for the federal government and for state and local agencies."
Kratos Defense divested its wireless assets in 2005-07.
The company's government solutions segment accounted for 79% of sales in Q3. Unmanned systems made up 21% of sales.
Kratos Defense & Security Solutions posted losses of 7 cents a share in 2015 and another 7 cents a share in 2016. The small-cap company then logged a 7-cents-a-share gain in 2017.
The Street expects a 200% earnings increase to 21 cents a share in 2018. Earnings are expected to jump 62% in 2019.
Stock Chart Kratos' stock chart has a sloppy look for the past couple of months, which is normal for the current stock market. The stock broke out Sept. 7, clearing its yearlong base. The buy point was 14.03.
The breakout failed when the loss from buy point reached 7% to 8% in mid-October. Since then, action has been jagged for both Kratos and the stock market. If the stock consolidates for at least six weeks, it will have put in enough time to form a cup-type base.
